archetype.name: Game Manager (turnover-prone)
archetype.definition: A short-area distributor who is supposed to keep a top-10 rushing offense on schedule with underneath throws, but who is giving the ball away far too often to manage anything.

report.headline: The 2025 breakout has evaporated; this is turnover-prone, short-area Jones again.
report.take:
Daniel Jones' career has had two genuinely good seasons, 2022 and 2025, surrounded by a lot of below-average football. Last year in Indianapolis he looked like a changed passer: 8.08 yards per attempt (7th), +0.193 EPA per play (11th), a +2.3 CPOE and a bad-throw rate among the league's best. Ten games into 2026, almost all of that is gone. He is at 5.65 yards per attempt (45th of 54), -0.172 EPA per dropback (42nd), a -5.84 CPOE, and his 12 interceptions are the most among qualifiers. This looks less like 2025 Jones in a slump and more like his 2023-24 baseline, only worse.

The decline is about accuracy and decisions, not volume or protection. His CPOE is down 8.1 points from last year and his bad-throw rate is up 3.7. He is also less aggressive (14.2% into tight windows vs 17.7%), so he is missing more of the throws he does choose. The vertical game has collapsed: 4 completions-worth of production on 35 deep attempts, an 11.4% completion rate and -0.472 EPA per throw. Throws of 10+ air yards have produced 7 interceptions and no touchdowns. The result is the league's worst passing offense (32nd in pass EPA) attached to the 7th-best rushing offense. The run game is carrying the Colts, and Jones is mostly not hurting them when he throws short.

The raw numbers hide a few things. His sack rate (7.2%) is actually better than the qualifier average, and his pressure-to-sack rate sits mid-pack, so this is not a pocket-collapse story. The intermediate game is quietly his best area at +0.084 EPA per attempt; the problem is that those same throws carry 5 interceptions. The target tree splits sharply. Josh Downs (+0.232 per target) and Keenan Allen produce, while Tyler Warren (-0.226 per target, 55 targets) and Jonathan Taylor's targets drain value. Even 'garbage' looks bad: leading by 9+, he's been dreadful on a tiny sample, and trailing by 9+ he's -0.305 per play, so there is no padding coming from soft-coverage scripts.

The direction is the worst part. Over the last three games he's at -0.359 EPA per dropback with a 6.0% interception rate and a -9.7 CPOE. The Miami win was his worst passing day by CPOE (-18.6), and Bernhard Raimann left that game with a concussion. With right tackle Jalen Travis also out, a short-week division road game is arriving at the worst possible moment for a passer whose margin is already gone.

strengths.title: Short game keeps him afloat
strengths.body: Under 10 air yards he completes about two-thirds of his throws and is roughly break-even, with a 50% success rate and all 7 of his touchdown passes. That is the part of the offense Shane Steichen can still lean on alongside a productive run game. It is sustainable because it fits what he has always been: a sub-8 aDOT passer whose best years came when he was efficient underneath.

strengths.title: Short-yardage legs still work
strengths.body: His designed runs are low-yardage (1.79 per carry) but hugely efficient: +0.464 EPA per play and a 78.6% success rate. That profile is short-yardage conversions, not open-field running. His scrambling is no longer a weapon at -0.196 EPA per scramble, so this is a narrow tool, but a real one near the sticks and goal line.

strengths.title: Downs and Allen remain productive
strengths.body: When the ball goes to his wideouts the offense works. Downs at +0.232 EPA per target and Allen at +0.135 are both comfortably positive in an offense that ranks last in passing. Both lean on timing and separation, which matches his best throws, and that should hold.

concerns.title: Interceptions are the defining problem
concerns.body: Twelve interceptions in ten starts rank dead last among 54 qualifiers. His 3.7% interception rate is well above the league's 2.5%, and it has been 6.0% over the last three games. Some of this is variance on 5 intermediate picks, but his bad-throw rate has risen alongside it, so expect the rate to ease rather than normalize. Five turnover-worthy fumbles add to the giveaway problem.

concerns.title: Accuracy collapse from last season
concerns.body: His CPOE is down 8.1 points from 2025 and his yards per attempt down 2.43, while time to throw barely moved. That points to ball placement, not a slower process. The vertical game is where it shows most: an 11.4% completion rate and a -26.4 CPOE on deep throws. His career says 2025 was the outlier, so a full rebound is unlikely, though the deep numbers should drift up from rock bottom.

concerns.title: Both starting tackles compromised
concerns.body: Jalen Travis (93% of snaps) is out, and Bernhard Raimann (89%) is in the concussion protocol on a four-day turnaround. Jones has handled pressure about league-average this year. But his last five games already carried a 9.8% sack rate, and the team's hit rate allowed ranks 26th. Backup tackles on both edges would push him into more rushed, inaccurate throws, the exact failure mode of his season.

trend.note: His only positive-EPA game came in Week 2 at Kansas City. Since Week 6 every efficiency measure has slid, bottoming out in the last three games at -0.359 EPA per dropback, with Week 10 his worst game by CPOE.

nextGame.headline: Short week, two hurt tackles, at Houston as an 11.5-point underdog
nextGame.body:
Houston's defense is middle-of-the-pack overall (17th in EPA) but generates sacks at the second-highest rate in the league, which is the worst possible trait to meet with a compromised line. Its weakness is exactly the area Jones can't exploit: the Texans allow a lot of deep and explosive passing (24th in deep EPA, 29th in explosive pass rate), and they are a mild pass funnel. Jones' deep game has produced almost nothing all year. The more realistic avenue is volume to his second receiver, since WR2s have run well above their averages against this defense. Tight ends have been held well under theirs, which is bad news for a Warren-heavy plan. As 11.5-point underdogs the Colts likely trail, but his trailing-by-9+ splits are poor, so extra volume doesn't promise efficiency. When these teams met in Week 3 he threw for 235 but took 4 sacks and lost 2 fumbles.

Availability cuts both ways. Indianapolis is without Travis, Raimann is unlikely to clear the protocol on a short week, and the tight end room is thin with Mo Alie-Cox on IR and Will Mallory out, so Warren plays even more. Houston is missing edge rusher Danielle Hunter (76% of snaps) and linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair (94%). That takes some heat off the backup tackles and some range out of the middle of the field. On offense the Texans lose Marvin Harrison Jr. and likely Woody Marks, which could slow their scoring a little, but the Book still prices this as a comfortable Houston win.

keyMatchups.title: Texans pass rush vs backup tackles
keyMatchups.body: Houston ranks 2nd in sack rate and 8th in hit rate. Jones may face it without both starting tackles. Hunter's absence softens it, but this is the matchup most likely to turn a bad passing day into a turnover-filled one.

keyMatchups.title: Soft WR2 coverage, stingy on TEs
keyMatchups.body: Second receivers have scored well over their averages against Houston, while top tight ends have been held well under. Steering targets to Downs or Allen and away from Warren is the efficient path. With the TE depth gone, though, the Colts may not have the bodies to do it.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots into a leaky secondary
keyMatchups.body: Houston gives up big plays downfield, but Jones' deep attempts have been the least productive part of his game. A couple of connections would change his day. More misses and picks are the likelier outcome given his current form.

nextGame.watch: How often he's hit early with backup tackles in. If the pocket holds, he can live underneath; if not, expect the interception rate to stay at last-three-game levels.

restOfSeason.body:
The sustainable part of Jones' game is the short, on-schedule passing behind a strong run game, plus enough volume to keep yardage around the league median. That supports something like 160 to 210 passing yards a game. The 2025 efficiency is not coming back on this evidence: his CPOE, bad-throw rate and aggressiveness have all moved the wrong way, and his career outside 2022 and 2025 looks much more like this. Some numbers should regress toward him. A 2.2% touchdown rate is low even for him, and an 11.4% deep completion rate can't stay that low. That points to modestly better TD output and an interception rate that eases toward one a game.

The floor is the offensive line. If Travis and Raimann miss time, the sack and turnover numbers from his last five games become the baseline rather than the dip. His rushing gives little fantasy cushion beyond short-yardage carries. In fantasy he is a low-floor, low-ceiling passer whose good weeks depend on Downs and Allen getting volume against soft secondaries.
swingFactors: How long Travis and Raimann are out
Whether the interception rate cools from its last-three-game spike
Target share shifting from Warren toward Downs and Allen

confidence.note: Ten starts with a consistent, career-backed decline; tackle injuries add short-term uncertainty.
